goldens.comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

golden_verdicts.matched_finding: V2 deployments lack entity-removal cleanup for admin permissions
golden_verdicts.reason: F5 identifies the same issue: AdminPermissions.registerListener is guarded by V1 feature flag, leaving V2 deployments without cleanup, leading to orphaned permissions.

golden_verdicts.matched_finding: V1→V2 resource name and type divergence in shared ResourceServer — no migration logic
golden_verdicts.reason: F10 and F13 both identify that hasPermission uses findByName with client.getId() (bare id) but V1 stored resources under 'client.resource.{id}', causing lookups to fail and fall back to all-clients resource.
F12 directly identifies that getClientsWithPermission returns resource.getName() (which is 'Clients') instead of client IDs, matching G2's description of the same bug.

findings.blocking_reason: The finding describes a hypothetical risk of a future implementation choice; the current code throws (fail-closed) and does not introduce a silent bypass or any exploitable vulnerability in this PR.
findings.body:
The critical token-exchange finding recommends three fix options, with Option 1 ('Implement canExchangeTo in V2 — evaluate against the schema') listed as preferred. Independently implementing that option would inherit the V1→V2 resource name/type divergence already documented for the general hasPermission path, and the token-exchange path is the worst place for that inheritance to surface.

Compound chain (verified in repo):
1. V1 ClientPermissions.canExchangeTo (line 328-370) enforces per-client token-exchange by looking up getResourceName(to) = "client.resource." + to.getId() and the permission getExchangeToPermissionName(to) = "token-exchange.permission.client." + to.getId() on the shared realmResourceServer. The resource is created with type "Client" (ClientPermissions.java line 132).
2. V2 ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 207-235) performs lookups using resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()) — bare client.getId() as resource name — and falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE = "Clients" (type-level) when the per-client resource is not found (lines 214-222). AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveClient (line 175-184) confirms the V2 schema canonicalizes the client resource name to the bare client.getId().
3. There is NO migration logic: a repo-wide search for "client.resource." and migrat inside services/.../admin/permissions returns only the V1 prefix constant itself (ClientPermissions.java:67,82). When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled on a realm that previously had V1 admin permissions configured, V1 resources (name client.resource.<id>, type Client) and V1 token-exchange policies (token-exchange.permission.client.<id>) remain in the shared ResourceServer but are unreachable by V2's lookup scheme.
4. The critical finding's preferred fix (Option 1) is to implement ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo by 'evaluating against the schema'. Any natural V2 implementation would mirror hasPermission (line 207-235): findByName(server, to.getId(), server.getId()), then fall back to the CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE type-level resource. Both lookups miss the V1-stored per-client resource and policy.

Resulting compound behavior, worse than either finding alone:
- If a V2 canExchangeTo follows the V2 lookup pattern and the realm has a type-level Clients policy that permits exchange (or no type-level policy, in which case hasPermission returns false at line 220-221): the per-client token-exchange.permission.client.<id> policy configured by an operator under V1 is silently ignored. A cross-client token exchange that V1 denied at the per-client level is now allowed (type-level permit) or uniformly denied (no type-level policy) — in both cases diverging from the operator's configured intent with no error, no log, and no migration warning.
- This is strictly worse than the current crash (Finding B alone): a crash is visible, fail-closed, and forces investigation. A silent bypass on the token-exchange authorization boundary is a security regression that an individual reviewer fixing the crash would not detect unless they also traced the resource-name divergence (Finding D) into the new implementation.
- The same compound applies to the 2-arg canExchangeTo(ClientModel, ClientModel) and to any future V2 implementation of the test-only throwing methods (exchangeToPermission, mapRolesPermission, etc.) that reuse hasPermission semantics.

Why an individual reviewer would miss this: Finding B frames the fix as 'implement the method in V2'. Finding D frames the impact as 'V1 permissions become invisible to V2 hasPermission'. Neither finding connects that the suggested fix for B is the exact operation that would propagate D's silent-bypass behavior onto the security-critical token-exchange authorization decision. The token-exchange boundary is also the path most likely to be exercised first under V2 (because TOKEN_EXCHANGE and ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 are independent feature flags and TOKEN_EXCHANGE has no V2 provider implementation), so this is the first place the divergence becomes exploitable rather than merely a degraded admin-permissions UX.
findings.evidence:
V1 enforcement: ClientPermissions.java:81-83 (getResourceName = "client.resource." + client.getId()), :104-106 (getExchangeToPermissionName = TOKEN_EXCHANGE + ".permission.client." + client.getId()), :132 (resource.setType("Client")), :328-370 (canExchangeTo uses these names for findByName + policy lookup + evaluatePermission).
V2 lookup: ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 (resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())), :217-221 (fallback to AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE type-level resource; returns false if no type-level policy), :244 (type-only hasPermission uses findByName(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)).
V2 schema canonical name: AdminPermissionsSchema.java:55 (CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE = "Clients"), :68 (CLIENTS ResourceType uses scopes CONFIGURE/MANAGE/MAP_ROLES/MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE/MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE/VIEW — note TOKEN_EXCHANGE is NOT in the V2 CLIENTS scope set), :175-184 (resolveClient returns bare client.getId()), :94 (schema resource name = resolveClient(session, id)).
Shared ResourceServer: MgmtPermissions.resourceServer returns realmResourceServer(client) (shared) — confirmed in finding D evidence; V1 and V2 write/read the same server.
No migration: grep for migrat and "client.resource." in services/.../admin/permissions returns only V1's own constant. No startup migration, no V1→V2 resource rename, no warning.
Call chain to canExchangeTo: AbstractTokenExchangeProvider.java:276 (AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(client, targetClient, token)) → AdminPermissions.java:66-68 (returns MgmtPermissionsV2 when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 on) → MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() → ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo:148 (currently throws).
Additional aggravation: V2 CLIENTS ResourceType scope set (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:68) does NOT include TOKEN_EXCHANGE, so a schema-conformant V2 canExchangeTo has no defined scope to evaluate — pushing any implementer toward the type-level fallback, which is exactly the silent-bypass path.
findings.suggestion:
Do not implement V2 canExchangeTo in isolation. Any fix for the token-exchange crash must be coupled with the resource-name/type migration from Finding D, AND with a V2 schema decision for the TOKEN_EXCHANGE scope (currently absent from the V2 CLIENTS ResourceType scope set at AdminPermissionsSchema.java:68). Concretely, in order of preference:
1. Block the fix: at AbstractTokenExchangeProvider.java:276, short-circuit to V1 ClientPermissions when the target client's resource was created under V1 naming (or simply when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on but no V2-named resource exists for the client). This keeps V1 per-client enforcement active and fails closed until a migration runs.
2. Add a V1→V2 migration (resource rename client.resource.<id> → <id>, type Client → Clients, policy rename token-exchange.permission.client.<id> → V2 schema policy) executed at V2 feature enablement, with a startup warning if V1 resources are detected and no migration has run. Only after migration succeeds should V2 canExchangeTo be permitted to evaluate.
3. Extend the V2 CLIENTS ResourceType to include a TOKEN_EXCHANGE scope (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:68) so a schema-conformant V2 implementation has a defined scope to evaluate instead of silently falling back to the type-level resource.
4. Until 1-3 are done, prefer the critical finding's Option 2 or Option 3 (gate the V1 call at AbstractTokenExchangeProvider:276, or make V1TokenExchangeProviderFactory.isSupported() return false when V2 admin is on) over Option 1 — those options do not introduce the silent bypass.
findings.title: Fixing the V2 canExchangeTo crash via the suggested 'implement in V2' option would silently bypass per-client token-exchange restrictions due to V1→V2 resource name/type divergence and missing migration

findings.blocking_reason: Cross-client token exchange path throws UnsupportedOperationException, causing a 500 error on a security-critical code path reachable in a valid production feature configuration.
findings.body:
**Reachable production path to a throwing V2 method.**

`ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo(ClientModel, ClientModel, AccessToken)` (line 148) throws `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. This method IS reachable in production when two independently-enabledable features are both on:

- **`TOKEN_EXCHANGE`** (V1 token exchange, `Profile.Feature.TOKEN_EXCHANGE`, Type.PREVIEW, **no dependencies** — Profile.java line 76)
- **`ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2`** (V2 admin permissions, Profile.java line 58)

These are **different unversioned feature keys** (`token-exchange` vs `admin-fine-grained-authz`), so the Profile framework's mutual-exclusion check (Profile.java lines 283-286, which only prevents two versions of the *same* unversioned key) does NOT prevent this combination. A deployment can legitimately enable V1 token exchange while upgrading admin permissions to V2.

**Call chain:**
1. `V1TokenExchangeProviderFactory.isSupported()` (line 60) returns true when `TOKEN_EXCHANGE` is on → provider is registered
2. `V1TokenExchangeProvider.tokenExchange()` (line 154) calls `exchangeClientToClient(tokenUser, tokenSession, token, ...)` — **does NOT override** this method, so dispatch goes to `AbstractTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToClient`
3. `AbstractTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToClient` (line 276): `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(client, targetClient, token)` — **NO feature gate** around this call
4. `AdminPermissions.management()` (line 67) returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is on
5. `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` (line 66) returns `new ClientPermissionsV2(...)`
6. `ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo(ClientModel, ClientModel, AccessToken)` (line 148) → **throws `UnsupportedOperationException`**

**Result:** Any cross-client token exchange (where `targetClient != client`, i.e., the `audience` parameter points to a different client) returns a **500 Internal Server Error** instead of a proper permission evaluation. Token exchange is a **security-critical path** — the permission check is meant to allow/deny, not crash.

**Why V2 token exchange providers don't help:** `StandardTokenExchangeProviderFactory`, `FederatedTokenExchangeProviderFactory`, and `SubjectImpersonationTokenExchangeProviderFactory` all depend on `Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1), NOT V2 (Profile.java lines 77-79). When V2 admin is on, V1 is off (mutual exclusion), so these V2 token exchange factories' `isSupported()` returns false. `V1TokenExchangeProvider` is the **only** token exchange provider active in this configuration.

**The 2-arg `canExchangeTo(ClientModel, ClientModel)` is also broken:** V1 `ClientPermissions.canExchangeTo` (2-arg) delegates to the 3-arg version, which virtual-dispatches to V2's throwing override. So both signatures are affected.
findings.dimension_name: V2 UnsupportedOperationException reachability under ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature
findings.evidence:
Step 1: V1TokenExchangeProvider.tokenExchange() line 154: `return exchangeClientToClient(tokenUser, tokenSession, token, disallowOnHolderOfTokenMismatch);` — calls inherited method, no override in V1TokenExchangeProvider (verified: 169-line file, only overrides supports() and tokenExchange()).
Step 2: AbstractTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToClient line 276: `if (!AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(client, targetClient, token))` — inside a loop over targetAudienceClients where targetClient != client (line 271 branch). No feature gate.
Step 3: AdminPermissions.management() line 67: `return new MgmtPermissionsV2(session, realm, authz)` when `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2)` is true.
Step 4: MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() line 66: `clientPermissions = new ClientPermissionsV2(session, realm, authz, this);` — returns ClientPermissionsV2 instance.
Step 5: ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo(ClientModel, ClientModel, AccessToken) line 148: `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2");`
Step 6: UnsupportedOperationException propagates uncaught through exchangeClientToClient → tokenExchange() → token exchange endpoint → 500 Internal Server Error.

Feature compatibility verified: TOKEN_EXCHANGE (Profile.java line 76, PREVIEW, no deps) and ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 (line 58, EXPERIMENTAL, depends on AUTHORIZATION) have different unversioned keys ('token-exchange' vs 'admin-fine-grained-authz'), so Profile's mutual-exclusion check (lines 283-286) does not block this combination.
findings.suggestion:
Three options, in order of preference:

1. **Implement `canExchangeTo` in V2** — evaluate against the schema (e.g., using a `TOKEN_EXCHANGE` scope or reusing `MANAGE` scope on the target client resource). This is the correct fix: V2 should provide a schema-based permission evaluation, not throw.

2. **Gate the V1 token exchange call at AbstractTokenExchangeProvider line 276** — wrap in `if (!Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2))` and provide an alternative permission check for V2 (or default-deny). This prevents the UOE but leaves token exchange non-functional under V2 admin.

3. **Make `V1TokenExchangeProviderFactory.isSupported()` return false when V2 admin is on** — add `&& !Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2)` to line 60. This disables V1 token exchange entirely under V2 admin, but leaves no token exchange provider available (since V2 token exchange factories depend on V1 admin). This is the safest stopgap but breaks token exchange for V2 admin users.

The TODO comments at Profile.java lines 77-79 ("TODO: Switch v2 token exchanges to depend admin-fine-grained-authz-v2") confirm this gap is known but unresolved.
findings.title: V1 token exchange reaches V2 canExchangeTo → UnsupportedOperationException on cross-client exchange

findings.blocking_reason: The PR introduces a runtime NPE on a reachable code path: returning resource name "Clients" causes realm.getClientById("Clients") to return null, then .getRolesStream() throws.
findings.body:
**holds=false** — The property does NOT hold. I verified in the real code at both ends:

- **Changed location** (`ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission:138-142`): adds `resource.getName()` to the returned set for every resource of type "Clients" with a granted permission.
- **Other end** (`AdminPermissionsSchema.init:247-252`): creates an all-clients resource with `name="Clients"` and `type="Clients"`. `JPAResourceStore.findByType:248-276` queries by type+owner and returns it.
- **Caller** (`AvailableRoleMappingResource:230`): `realm.getClientById("Clients")` returns null → NPE on `.getRolesStream()`.

Additionally, per-client resources created via `getOrCreateResource:104` never have `type="Clients"` set, so `findByType("Clients")` only returns the all-clients resource — compounding the bug.
findings.evidence: ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission:138-142, AdminPermissionsSchema.init:247-252, JPAResourceStore.findByType:248-276, AvailableRoleMappingResource:230, getOrCreateResource:104
findings.title: The property does NOT hold

findings.blocking_reason: The finding is about missing diagnostic telemetry/logging to distinguish failure modes, which is an observability improvement, not a build break, security vulnerability, data loss, API contract break, or regression of previously working behavior.
findings.body:
When an operator enables ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 on a realm that previously used V1 admin permissions AND uses token exchange, two independent failure modes activate simultaneously and present identical symptoms with no way to distinguish them:

**Failure mode A (Finding 1):** Cross-client token exchange returns 500 Internal Server Error because `canExchangeTo` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. The operator sees server-side 500s and `Errors.NOT_ALLOWED` is never reached (the UOE propagates before the `event.error` call at AbstractTokenExchangeProvider:278).

**Failure mode B (Finding 3):** If the operator attempts to inspect or repair permissions via the admin UI, `getClientsWithPermission` (ClientPermissionsV2.java:138) queries `findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` = type `"Clients"`. V1 resources are typed `"Client"` (singular). The query returns an empty set, so the admin UI shows ZERO clients with token-exchange (or any) permissions granted — even though the V1 resources still exist in the shared ResourceServer. The operator concludes no permissions are configured.

The diagnostic trap: the operator cannot determine whether token exchange is failing because (a) the V2 canExchangeTo method is unimplemented (Finding 1) or (b) V2 cannot see the V1 permission resources that are still present (Finding 3). Both manifest as 'token exchange doesn't work'. The admin UI's empty permission list (Failure mode B) actively misleads the operator toward believing the permissions simply were never configured, hiding the real V1 data. There is no log message in `hasPermission`'s null-resource branch (line 215) or in `getClientsWithPermission` that distinguishes 'no V2 resources exist' from 'V1 resources exist but are invisible due to type/name mismatch'.

The shared ResourceServer (MgmtPermissions.resourceServer delegates to realmResourceServer, used by both V1 and V2) makes this worse: V1 resources physically persist in the store, so the operator's 'missing permissions' conclusion is factually wrong — the data is there, just unreachable through any V2 code path. A rollback to V1 would restore visibility, but the operator has no signal that a rollback would help, since V2 reports a clean (empty) state rather than a corrupted state.
findings.evidence: AbstractTokenExchangeProvider.java:276 — `canExchangeTo` call is not wrapped in try/catch; UOE propagates uncaught, producing 500 before the `event.error(Errors.NOT_ALLOWED)` at line 278. ClientPermissionsV2.java:138-148 — `getClientsWithPermission` uses `findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` where CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE = "Clients" (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:55); V1 resources typed "Client" (ClientPermissions.java:132) are excluded → empty result. ClientPermissionsV2.java:215 — null-resource branch in `hasPermission` has no log statement distinguishing 'no resource for this client' from 'no all-clients policy'. MgmtPermissions.java:245-246 — `resourceServer(ClientModel)` delegates to `realmResourceServer()`, shared by V1 and V2 (confirmed in Finding 3 evidence). No grep hits for migration logic referencing "client.resource." prefix (only ClientPermissions.java:67,82).
findings.suggestion: Add distinguishing telemetry at the V2/V1 boundary: (1) In `getClientsWithPermission`, after the type-"Clients" query returns empty, run a secondary `findByType(server, "Client")` query and log a WARNING if it returns non-empty: 'N V1 client permission resources detected but invisible to V2 — enable migration or roll back to V1'. (2) In `hasPermission`'s null-resource branch (line 215), log at DEBUG/TRACE whether a V1-named resource (`"client.resource." + client.getId()`) exists in the same server, so operators can confirm V1 data is present-but-invisible. (3) In `canExchangeTo` (line 148), before throwing UOE, log a distinct ERROR mentioning the TOKEN_EXCHANGE + ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 feature combination so the 500's server log is self-diagnosing rather than a bare stack trace.
findings.title: V2 token-exchange failure is undiagnosable: UOE crash and silent V1-permission invisibility present identical operator symptoms with no distinguishing telemetry

findings.blocking_reason: The finding describes an intended behavioral change with a missing test for the deny-case, which is a test coverage gap, not a demonstrated security vulnerability or regression.
findings.body:
**V2 `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` (lines 214-222)** introduces a fall-back that **does not exist in V1** and **changes the deny-by-default semantics** of `canManage`/`canConfigure`/`canView`/`canMapRoles`/`canMapCompositeRoles`/`canMapClientScopeRoles`.

**V1 behavior** (`ClientPermissions.canManage` line 384-388, `canConfigure` line 412-416, `hasView` line 458-462, `canMapRoles` line 537-541, `canMapCompositeRoles` line 614-618, `canMapClientScopeRoles` line 636-640): each resolves `resourceServer(client)` and `findByName(server, getResourceName(client))` (the per-client resource named `client.resource.<id>`). If **either is null**, the method returns `false` with **no fall-back**. A client with no per-client resource is **deny-by-default** for all six scopes.

**V2 behavior** (`ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission` line 214-222): resolves `resource = resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())`. If `resource == null`, it falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` — the **all-clients** "Clients" resource. If `policyStore.findByResource(server, <all-clients-resource>)` is **non-empty**, it evaluates the permission against the **all-clients resource** and returns `true` if the requested scope is granted.

**The broadening:** a client with **no per-client resource** — which V1 **denies** for all scopes — can now be **granted** `canManage`/`canConfigure`/`canView`/`canMapRoles`/`canMapCompositeRoles`/`canMapClientScopeRoles` via a permission configured on the all-clients "Clients" resource type. This is the **intended new feature** (admins can grant permissions that apply to all clients), but it is a **semantic change from V1** that is **not covered by tests** for the deny-case.

**Test gap:** `PermissionClientTest.testManageAllClients` (line 250) creates an all-clients `MANAGE` permission and verifies the admin can create/list/delete clients — this exercises the **grant** path of the fall-back. However, **no test** verifies the **deny-case**: that an all-clients permission for scope `VIEW` does **not** grant `MANAGE`/`CONFIGURE`/`MAP_ROLES` for a client with no per-client resource. Without this test, a regression in the evaluation logic (e.g. the missing `resourceId` guard described in the companion finding) could silently grant broader access than intended.

**Combinations that differ (V1 → V2) for a client with no per-client resource:**

| All-clients permission | V1 `canManage` | V2 `canManage` |
|---|---|---|
| None | `false` (line 388) | `false` (line 220 — `findByResource` empty) |
| Grants `MANAGE` | `false` (line 388) | **`true`** (fall-back evaluates, scope matches) |
| Grants `CONFIGURE` only | `false` (line 388) | `false` for `MANAGE`, **`true`** for `canConfigure` (line 61) |
| Grants `VIEW` only | `false` (line 388) | `false` for `MANAGE`/`CONFIGURE`, **`true`** for `canView` (line 82) |
| Grants `MAP_ROLES` only | `false` (line 541) | **`true`** for `canMapRoles` (line 92) |

The same broadening applies to `canMapCompositeRoles` (line 96) and `canMapClientScopeRoles` (line 101).
findings.dimension_name: V2 hasPermission fall-back grants where V1 denies
findings.evidence:
Step 1: V1 `ClientPermissions.canManage(ClientModel)` line 384-388: `ResourceServer server = resourceServer(client); if (server == null) return false; Resource resource = authz.getStoreFactory().getResourceStore().findByName(server, getResourceName(client)); if (resource == null) return false;` — NO fall-back, returns false.
Step 2: V2 `ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` line 214-222: `Resource resource = resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()); if (resource == null) { resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE); if (authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()) { return false; } }` — falls back to all-clients resource.
Step 3: V2 line 224-232: `Collection<Permission> permissions = root.evaluatePermission(new ResourcePermission(resource, resource.getScopes(), server), server); ... for (String s : permission.getScopes()) { if (expectedScopes.contains(s)) { return true; } }` — evaluates against the all-clients resource and returns true if scope matches.
Step 4: V2 `canManage(ClientModel)` line 65-68 calls `hasPermission(client, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)` which uses this fall-back. `canConfigure` line 58-61 calls `canManage` then `hasPermission(client, CONFIGURE)`. `canView(ClientModel)` line 77-82 calls `canView()` then `canConfigure(client)` then `hasPermission(client, VIEW)`. All route through the fall-back.
Step 5: `PermissionClientTest.java` — `testManageAllClients` (line 250) tests the grant path (all-clients MANAGE → can manage). No test asserts the deny path (all-clients VIEW → cannot manage/configure).
findings.suggestion: Add a test in `PermissionClientTest.java` that verifies the deny-case of the fall-back: create an all-clients permission granting only `VIEW`, then assert that `canManage(client)` and `canConfigure(client)` return `false` for a client with no per-client resource (e.g. by attempting a manage/configure operation via the admin client and expecting `ForbiddenException`). Also add a test verifying that an all-clients `MAP_ROLES` permission does not grant `MANAGE`/`VIEW`. This locks in the intended semantics and guards against future regressions in the evaluation path.
findings.title: Fall-back to all-clients resource broadens access vs V1 deny-by-default, with no test covering the deny-case of the fall-back

findings.blocking_reason: Not a regression (explicitly stated), no security vulnerability, no build break; orphaned resource accumulation is a data-quality/maintenance gap, not data loss or corruption with a demonstrated production impact.
findings.body:
The PR's `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))` gate around `AdminPermissions.registerListener` (line 77) leaves V2 deployments without entity-removal cleanup for admin permissions. Under V2, the listener dispatches into `MgmtPermissionsV2`/`ClientPermissionsV2`/`UserPermissionsV2` which all throw `UnsupportedOperationException` on `setPermissionsEnabled` — so for every `RoleRemovedEvent`, `ClientRemovedEvent`, and `GroupRemovedEvent`, the V1 cleanup that deleted 3-7 policies + the admin-permission Resource per entity is lost.

**Not a regression** — matches the `UserPermissionsV2` precedent (accepted V2 design limitation). But a real data-lifecycle gap: orphaned resources/policies accumulate indefinitely, only reaped if an admin manually deletes the corresponding policy (triggering `AdminPermissionsSchema.removeOrphanResources` from `ScopePolicyProviderFactory.java:83` or `RepresentationToModel.java:1463`). The `AuthorizationStoreFactory` Synchronizers handle only the UMA/resource-server subsystem, not admin permissions.
findings.evidence: 12 evidence entries covering: the flag gate, three V1 cleanup implementations, two V2 UnsupportedOperationException precedents, the schema-side orphan hooks and their only two callers, the Synchronizer registrations, and a uniqueness grep confirming `AdminPermissions.registerListener` is the sole handler for these events.
findings.title: V2 deployments lack entity-removal cleanup for admin permissions

findings.blocking_reason: The new fall-back path uses findByResource which can never find policies created via the standard admin REST flow (they only have defaultResourceType config, no direct resource association), so the all-clients permission check always returns empty and always denies, breaking the feature this PR introduces.
findings.body: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel, String), the fall-back path (lines 214-222) resolves the all-clients resource via AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and then checks authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty() to decide whether any all-clients permission exists. However, JPAPolicyStore.findByResource delegates to the named query 'findPolicyIdByResource' defined in PolicyEntity.java: "select p from PolicyEntity p inner join p.resources r where p.resourceServer.id = :serverId and (r.resourceServer = :serverId and r.id = :resourceId)". This is an INNER JOIN on the policy→resource association collection (p.resources), so it only returns policies that have a DIRECT resource association with the given Resource. Policies created via the test helper createAllPermission(client, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, policy, Set.of(MANAGE)) (AbstractPermissionTest.java:151-161) build a ScopePermissionRepresentation with .resourceType("Clients") and NO resources set, then POST it through the admin REST endpoint. In RepresentationToModel.toModel (server-spi-private/.../models/utils/RepresentationToModel.java:1229-1306), updateResources(resources, model, authorization) is called with resources=null (since representation.getResources() is null and the representation is a ScopePermissionRepresentation, not a PolicyRepresentation, so the config-based fallback at lines 1243-1253 does not apply). When resourceIds is null, updateResources skips the entire association block (line 1412 "if (resourceIds != null)") — so no Resource is linked to the policy. Afterwards, ScopePolicyProviderFactory.onCreate (services/.../authz/policy/common/ScopePolicyProviderFactory.java:72) calls updateResourceType, which only stores representation.getResourceType() into the policy config under the key "defaultResourceType" (lines 86-97). It does NOT associate any Resource with the Policy. The net result: the created Policy has defaultResourceType="Clients" in its config map, but an EMPTY p.resources collection. Such a policy is discoverable by PolicyStore.findByResourceType (whose named query 'findPolicyIdByResourceType' queries the config map for KEY(c)='defaultResourceType' and c like :type), but NOT by findByResource, which only inspects the p.resources join table. Consequently, in the changed fall-back path, findByResource(server, allClientsResource) will ALWAYS return an empty list for any all-clients permission created through the standard admin REST / test-helper flow, causing the fall-back to return false (deny) even when a valid all-clients MANAGE permission exists. This breaks the entire 'all-clients permission grants access to any client without a per-client resource' feature that the fall-back was introduced to support. The correct call should be findByResourceType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) (or equivalently findByScopes on the all-clients resource scopes), not findByResource on the all-clients Resource instance.
findings.title: Fall-back path uses findByResource but all-clients policies are only linked via defaultResourceType config, so the check always returns empty and always denies

findings.blocking_reason: Missing tests for new code paths, without evidence of broken build, existing regression, or demonstrated production impact.
findings.body: The PR adds canExchangeTo and exchangeToPermission to the ClientPermissionEvaluator interface. These are token-exchange authorization checks — a fundamentally different code path from admin REST operations. No test in any of the 5 files exercises token exchange with client-level permissions. PermissionClientTest tests admin REST operations exclusively (toRepresentation, update, findAll, generateNewSecret, getDefaultClientScopes, protocolMappers, roles). The token exchange path (where canExchangeTo decides if client A can exchange tokens for client B) is completely untested. This is especially risky because the all-clients vs per-client permission distinction could have different semantics in the exchange path vs the admin REST path.
findings.evidence: No test method in PermissionClientTest, PermissionRESTTest, UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest, or UserResourceTypePermissionTest references token exchange, exchangeTo, or canExchangeTo. The only token-related operations tested are admin REST operations on client resources.
findings.suggestion: Add a test method in PermissionClientTest that: (1) grants exchangeToPermission on a specific client, (2) attempts a token exchange from an authorized client, (3) verifies success, (4) attempts from an unauthorized client, (5) verifies denial. Also test the all-clients exchangeTo permission variant.
findings.title: No test for exchangeTo/canExchangeTo token exchange with client permissions

findings.blocking_reason: The failure requires simultaneously enabling a PREVIEW and an EXPERIMENTAL feature flag, the finding does not demonstrate this is a regression introduced by this PR, and the impact is a cleanup exception in a non-standard configuration rather than data loss or a contract break.
findings.body: The two AFGA flags are independent (V2 depends on `AUTHORIZATION`, not on V1). When both V1 and V2 are simultaneously enabled, the V1-guarded listener fires on `ClientRemovedEvent`, `management()` returns the V2 implementation, and `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, breaking client-removal cleanup. The same breakage applies to the `RoleRemovedEvent` (line 88) and `GroupRemovedEvent` (line 94) paths.
findings.evidence: `registerListener` guard at `AdminPermissions.java:77` fires cleanup body when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1) enabled. ClientRemovedEvent cleanup at `AdminPermissions.java:91` unconditionally calls `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false)`. `management()` factory at `AdminPermissions.java:66-71` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` enabled. V1 flag at `Profile.java:56` is PREVIEW, no dependencies. V2 flag at `Profile.java:58` is EXPERIMENTAL, depends on `Feature.AUTHORIZATION` (NOT on V1). V2 `setPermissionsEnabled` at `ClientPermissionsV2.java:192-195` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. V1 `clients()` at `MgmtPermissions.java:221-223` returns `ClientPermissions` (V1) which supports the op.
findings.suggestion: Gate the listener on the V2 flag first (skip or replace the V1-style cleanup when V2 is active), symmetric with how `management()` selects the implementation.
findings.title: Consistency bug in AdminPermissions cleanup when both AFGA V1 and V2 are enabled

findings.blocking_reason: This is a missing test coverage / negative-case testing suggestion, not a production code defect or behavior regression.
findings.body: testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient (line 280-366) grants USERS MAP_ROLES + client MAP_ROLES + MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE + CONFIGURE all at once, then verifies both addRole and addComposites succeed. This tests that the combined permission works, but does NOT test scope isolation: (1) No test verifies that MAP_ROLES alone (without MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE) is insufficient for addComposites — a user could potentially bypass the MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE requirement. (2) No test verifies that MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE alone (without MAP_ROLES) is insufficient for addRole. (3) No test verifies that CONFIGURE alone is insufficient for MAP_ROLES operations. The test only verifies the positive case (all scopes granted → all operations succeed), not the negative cases (subset of scopes → specific operations denied).
findings.evidence: Line 295-300: grants Set.of(MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, CONFIGURE) in a single createPermission call. Line 350-360: verifies both users().roles().clientLevel().add() and clients().roles().addComposites() succeed. No intermediate deny-check with reduced scope set.
findings.suggestion: Split into multiple test methods or add assertions within the existing test: (1) Grant only MAP_ROLES (not MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE) → verify addRole succeeds but addComposites is denied. (2) Grant only MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE (not MAP_ROLES) → verify addComposites succeeds but addRole is denied. (3) Grant only CONFIGURE → verify both MAP_ROLES operations are denied.
findings.title: testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient grants MAP_ROLES + MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE together — no scope isolation test

findings.blocking_reason: The issue is a V1→V2 migration gap behind an opt-in feature flag; existing V1 behavior is preserved when the flag is off, data is not destroyed (resources still exist but are not found by V2 lookups), and the security-broadening scenario is conditional on specific pre-existing configuration rather than a concrete reachable exploit.
findings.body:
V1 (ClientPermissions) and V2 (ClientPermissionsV2) share the SAME ResourceServer instance (MgmtPermissions.resourceServer(ClientModel) at line 245-246 delegates to realmResourceServer(), the realm-level admin-permissions client's resource server — identical to what V2 uses via root.realmResourceServer()). Despite sharing the store, V1 and V2 use incompatible resource naming AND type strings:

• V1 resource name: "client.resource." + client.getId()  (ClientPermissions.java line 82, RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX = "client.resource.")
• V2 resource name: client.getId()  (bare storage id, AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveClient line 175-184 returns client.getId())
• V1 resource type: "Client"  (ClientPermissions.java line 132)
• V2 resource type: "Clients"  (AdminPermissionsSchema.java line 55, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE = "Clients")

When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled (AdminPermissions.java lines 40-68 unconditionally returns MgmtPermissionsV2), V2's hasPermission lookup (line 214: resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())) will NOT find V1-created resources because their names are prefixed with "client.resource.". Similarly, getClientsWithPermission (V2 line 138: findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)) queries type "Clients" and will not enumerate V1 resources typed "Client". No migration script exists — a grep for "client.resource." across the entire codebase finds the literal only in ClientPermissions.java (V1), with no migration/import logic that renames or re-types existing resources.

Impact: If an operator enables the V2 feature flag on a realm that previously had V1 admin permissions configured, all per-client permission resources become invisible to V2. hasPermission silently falls through to the all-clients fallback (lines 215-222): if an all-clients policy exists, access may broaden unexpectedly; if not, all per-client permissions are effectively denied. getClientsWithPermission returns an empty set, so admin UI surfaces show no granted clients. This is silent data loss with no warning or log message.
findings.evidence: MgmtPermissions.java:245-246 — `public ResourceServer resourceServer(ClientModel client) { return realmResourceServer(); }` (V1 and V2 share the same store). AdminPermissions.java:40-41 — `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2)) { return new MgmtPermissionsV2(...); }` (V2 fully replaces V1 when flag on). ClientPermissions.java:82 — `return "client.resource." + client.getId();`. ClientPermissions.java:132 — `resource.setType("Client");`. AdminPermissionsSchema.java:55 — `CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE = "Clients"`. AdminPermissionsSchema.java:175-184 resolveClient returns `client.getId()` (bare). ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — `resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())` (bare id lookup). No migration script found referencing "client.resource." prefix.
findings.suggestion: Add a migration path (or at minimum a startup warning) that handles V1→V2 transition. Options: (1) On V2 enablement, scan for resources with type "Client" and name prefix "client.resource.", re-create them as type "Clients" with bare-name, and migrate attached policies. (2) Make V2 hasPermission fall back to V1 naming (try bare id first, then "client.resource." + id) so V1 resources remain visible during transition. (3) If V2 is intentionally a clean break, document that enabling V2 on a realm with existing V1 permissions requires reconfiguration, and log a WARNING when V2 is enabled on a realm where V1 resources (type "Client") are detected. At minimum, add a log statement in hasPermission's null-resource branch (line 215) that distinguishes 'no resource for this client' from 'no all-clients policy', so operators can diagnose silent permission loss.
findings.title: V1→V2 resource name and type divergence in shared ResourceServer — no migration logic

findings.blocking_reason: Missing test coverage for cross-resource-type isolation is a test gap, not a demonstrated production bug, regression, or contract break.
findings.body: The PR risk surfaces explicitly identify 'schema mutation safety on shared state' as a concern. AdminPermissionsSchema is shared state that now includes CLIENTS alongside USERS, GROUPS, REALM. testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient creates both USERS and CLIENTS permissions in the same test, but no test verifies that creating/modifying a CLIENTS permission does not affect USERS permissions (or vice versa). Specifically: (1) No test verifies that a CLIENTS permission grant doesn't inadvertently grant USERS access. (2) No test verifies that the schema's resource type lookup for CLIENTS doesn't corrupt the lookup for USERS. (3) No test verifies that permission evaluation for one resource type doesn't bleed into another. The @AfterEach cleanup removes ALL scope permissions (not just CLIENTS), which further obscures cross-resource-type interactions.
findings.evidence: Risk surfaces: 'schema mutation safety on shared state'. @AfterEach line 40-50: getScopePermissionsResource(client).findAll(null,null,null,-1,-1).forEach(p -> permissions.findById(p.getId()).remove()) — cleans ALL resource types. testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient creates USERS + CLIENTS permissions but only verifies positive access, not isolation.
findings.suggestion: Add a test that: (1) Creates a USERS permission granting VIEW to myadmin, (2) Creates a CLIENTS permission granting MANAGE to myadmin, (3) Verifies myadmin can access users (VIEW) but cannot MANAGE users, (4) Verifies myadmin can MANAGE clients but cannot VIEW users beyond what was granted. This tests that permissions for different resource types are properly isolated.
findings.title: No test for schema mutation safety — cross-resource-type permission isolation untested

findings.blocking_reason: The finding describes a correctness bug in new V2 code but does not concretely demonstrate it is a regression of previously working behavior or a break of an existing API contract that real callers depend on.
findings.body: schema's `getOrCreateResource` (line 104) never calls `resource.setType(...)`, so `findByType(server, "Clients")` only returns the all-clients aggregate, never actual per-client Resources. The method returns the literal string "Clients" instead of client IDs.
findings.dimension_name: Resource name resolution consistency between schema and per-client lookup
findings.title: V2 `getClientsWithPermission` cannot find per-client resources

findings.blocking_reason: Changing the permission lookup key format without a migration path is a behavioral regression that can either broaden or deny access compared to V1.
findings.body: V2 `hasPermission` looks up `findByName(server, client.getId())` (raw id) but V1 stored Resources under `"client.resource.{id}"` with type `"Client"`. V2 silently falls back to the all-clients aggregate, either broadening or denying access and ignoring V1 per-client config. No migration step exists.
findings.dimension_name: Resource name resolution consistency between schema and per-client lookup
findings.title: V1→V2 cutover

findings.blocking_reason: The finding itself confirms 11 of 12 methods are production-safe and the one critical path is addressed in a separate finding; this is a test-gating suggestion.
findings.body:
Full reachability analysis of all 12 `UnsupportedOperationException`-throwing methods in `ClientPermissionsV2`:

| Method | Line | Production Callers | V2-Reachable? | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `canExchangeTo(ClientModel, ClientModel, AccessToken)` | 148 | `AbstractTokenExchangeProvider:276` via V1TokenExchangeProvider | **YES** | **CRITICAL** — see separate finding |
| `exchangeToPermission(ClientModel)` | 153 | Tests only (FineGrainAdminUnitTest:1355, ClientTokenExchangeSAML2Test:201-204, TokenExchangeTestUtils:181) | No | Safe (tests will break under V2) |
| `mapRolesPermission(ClientModel)` | 158 | Tests only (FineGrainAdminUnitTest:281) | No | Safe |
| `mapRolesClientScopePermission(ClientModel)` | 163 | None found | No | Safe |
| `mapRolesCompositePermission(ClientModel)` | 168 | None found | No | Safe |
| `managePermission(ClientModel)` | 173 | Tests only (FineGrainAdminUnitTest:293) | No | Safe |
| `configurePermission(ClientModel)` | 178 | Tests only (FineGrainAdminUnitTest:306) | No | Safe |
| `viewPermission(ClientModel)` | 183 | None found | No | Safe |
| `isPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel)` | 188 | `ClientResource:710` — V1-gated (ProfileHelper.requireFeature at line 706) | No | Safe — V1 gate blocks when V2 is on |
| `setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean)` | 193 | `ClientResource:742` — V1-gated (line 739); `AdminPermissions:91` — V1-gated (registerListener line 77) | No | Safe — V1 gate blocks when V2 is on |
| `resource(ClientModel)` | 198 | `ClientResource:719` — V1-gated (line 706) | No | Safe |
| `getPermissions(ClientModel)` | 203 | `ClientResource:720` — V1-gated (line 706) | No | Safe |

**Key mitigations verified:**

1. **`AdminPermissions.registerListener` (line 77):** The `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))` guard wraps ALL three event branches (RoleRemoved L78, ClientRemoved L89, GroupRemoved L92). When V2 is on, V1 is off (mutual exclusion — Profile.java lines 283-286), so the entire listener body is skipped. The `setPermissionsEnabled(client, false)` call at line 91 is NOT reached under V2. ✅

2. **`ClientResource` management permission endpoints (lines 706, 739):** Both `getManagementPermissions()` and `setManagementPermissionsEnabled()` call `ProfileHelper.requireFeature(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` — the V1 flag. When V2 is on, V1 is off, so these endpoints are blocked before reaching any throwing method. ✅

3. **`MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` (line 66):** Confirmed returns `new ClientPermissionsV2(session, realm, authz, this)` — V2 is only instantiated when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is on (AdminPermissions.java line 67). No code path instantiates MgmtPermissionsV2 without the feature flag. ✅

**Unblocked risk:** The `canExchangeTo` path (separate critical finding) is the ONLY production-reachable throwing method. The 6 permission-management methods (`exchangeToPermission`, `mapRolesPermission`, `managePermission`, `configurePermission`, `viewPermission`, `mapRolesClientScope/CompositePermission`) are only called from tests, meaning test suites exercising fine-grained permission setup will fail under V2 but production code is safe.
findings.dimension_name: V2 UnsupportedOperationException reachability under ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature
findings.evidence: Grep across entire repo for `.clients().setPermissionsEnabled(`, `.clients().isPermissionsEnabled(`, `.clients().resource(`, `.clients().getPermissions(`, `.clients().managePermission(`, `.clients().configurePermission(`, `.clients().viewPermission(`, `.clients().mapRolesPermission(`, `.clients().mapRolesClientScopePermission(`, `.clients().mapRolesCompositePermission(`, `.clients().canExchangeTo(`, `.clients().exchangeToPermission(` — 25 matches in 5 files. Production files: ClientResource.java (4 calls, V1-gated), AdminPermissions.java (1 call, V1-gated). Test files: FineGrainAdminUnitTest.java (10 calls), ClientTokenExchangeSAML2Test.java (7 calls), TokenExchangeTestUtils.java (2 calls). AbstractTokenExchangeProvider.java:276 (canExchangeTo, NOT gated) — the sole critical path. MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() confirmed at line 66 to return ClientPermissionsV2.
findings.suggestion: For the 6 test-only methods: consider providing V2 implementations or marking the tests as V1-only with `@DisableForFeature(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2)` to avoid test failures when running under V2. The V2 design intentionally replaces per-client permission resource management with schema-based evaluation, so these methods may never be implemented in V2 — but the tests should be explicitly gated rather than left to crash.
findings.title: Reachability verification complete for all 12 throwing methods — 1 critical path found, 11 verified safe under V2

findings.blocking_reason: This is an architectural suggestion about future implementation risks for methods that currently throw UnsupportedOperationException and are not reachable from production code paths.
findings.body:
Finding 0 documents that 6 permission-management methods (`exchangeToPermission`, `mapRolesPermission`, `mapRolesClientScopePermission`, `mapRolesCompositePermission`, `managePermission`, `configurePermission`, `viewPermission`) are called only from tests and throw `UnsupportedOperationException` under V2, and suggests providing V2 implementations or gating the tests. Finding 3 documents the V1→V2 resource name/type divergence with no migration. These combine into a systemic control gap: each test failure is an invitation to implement the method in V2, and every V2 implementation that follows the existing `hasPermission` pattern (bare-id lookup at line 214) will silently miss V1 resources.

The pattern is uniform: all 6 methods in V1 (ClientPermissions.java) look up resources via `getResourceName(client)` = `"client.resource." + client.getId()` (lines 207, 302, 387, 415, 461, 540, 617, 639 — 8 call sites). The V2 `hasPermission` counterpart uses bare `client.getId()`. An implementer fixing test failures one method at a time has no single place that enforces V1-name awareness — each new V2 method is an independent silent-failure point. Worse, the tests themselves (FineGrainAdminUnitTest, ClientTokenExchangeSAML2Test) set up V1-style permissions, so a V2 implementation that passes against fresh V2 fixtures will still fail against V1-fixture tests, but the failure mode shifts from a loud UOE to a silent wrong-result (broadening or denial) that the test may not assert against correctly.

This is a systemic control gap rather than a single bug: the codebase has no shared helper that abstracts V1/V2 resource-name resolution, no migration step, and no test harness that exercises V2 implementations against V1-created data. Each of the 6 methods is a separate trapdoor.
findings.evidence: ClientPermissionsV2.java:153-183 — 6 methods throw UOE (Finding 0's test-only set). ClientPermissions.java:207,302,387,415,461,540,617,639 — 8 V1 call sites using `findByName(server, getResourceName(client))` where getResourceName returns prefixed name (line 82). ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — V2 uses bare-id `findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())`. No shared resource-name resolver exists (grep for `getResourceName` shows it only in ClientPermissions.java, not inherited or reused by V2). Finding 0 suggestion: 'consider providing V2 implementations or marking the tests as V1-only' — the first option is the trapdoor.
findings.suggestion: Introduce a single shared resource-lookup helper (e.g., `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveResource(server, client)`) that tries V2 bare-id first and falls back to V1 `"client.resource." + id`, used by ALL V2 permission methods including the 6 test-only ones and any future canExchangeTo implementation. This closes the systemic gap with one abstraction instead of patching 7+ independent methods. Pair with a migration test that creates V1 resources, enables V2, and asserts V2 lookups still find them via the helper. Without a shared resolver, each method implementation is a separate silent-failure vector.
findings.title: Six test-only throwing methods create an implementation breadcrumb that repeatedly leads into the V1→V2 resource-name migration trap

findings.blocking_reason: This is an intended V2 design change with a deny-by-default gate at line 219 (no policies = deny), and the suggested fix is documentation and tests, not a correctness or security defect.
findings.body:
`ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` (line 211) resolves the `ResourceServer` via `root.realmResourceServer()` — the **realm-level** admin-permissions client's resource server. V1's `canManage(ClientModel)` (line 384) resolves via `resourceServer(client)` — the **per-client** resource server (delegating to `root.resourceServer(client)`).

This is a **fundamental design change**: V1 scoped authorization to the resource server owned by the target client (each client could host its own authorization metadata), while V2 centralizes all client authorization on the single realm admin-permissions client's resource server. This is consistent with the `AdminPermissionsSchema` design (which creates a single admin permissions client per realm at line 230 of `AdminPermissionsSchema.java`).

The implication for the fall-back broadening: in V1, a client that had **no resource server of its own** (`resourceServer(client)==null`) was denied at line 385 — the admin had to explicitly enable permissions on that client (`setPermissionsEnabled`) which called `initialize(client)` which created `root.findOrCreateResourceServer(client)`. In V2, the realm-level resource server is always used, so the per-client resource server is **never consulted** — the fall-back to the all-clients resource is the **only** path when no per-client resource exists on the realm server.

This means the V1 "deny because no resource server" case and the V1 "deny because no per-client resource" case **both** collapse into the V2 fall-back path. An admin who has **never enabled permissions on a specific client** (no `setPermissionsEnabled` call) but who has configured an all-clients permission will see that client become **accessible** under V2, where it was **inaccessible** under V1.

This is the intended behavior of the V2 schema-based design, but it represents a **migration concern**: realms upgrading from V1 to V2 where admins have configured all-clients permissions (or where the schema `init` creates the default all-clients resources at `AdminPermissionsSchema.init` line 247) may see previously-denied clients become accessible. The `AdminPermissionsSchema.init` method (line 222-255) automatically creates the all-clients "Clients" resource and all scopes when the admin permissions client is first initialized — so **every V2 realm has the all-clients resource by default**, meaning the fall-back path is **always reachable** for any client without a per-client resource.
findings.dimension_name: V2 hasPermission fall-back grants where V1 denies
findings.evidence:
Step 1: V1 `ClientPermissions.canManage(ClientModel)` line 384: `ResourceServer server = resourceServer(client);` — per-client resource server. Line 385: `if (server == null) return false;` — deny if client has no resource server.
Step 2: V2 `ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` line 211: `ResourceServer server = root.realmResourceServer();` — realm-level resource server (always the admin permissions client's server).
Step 3: `AdminPermissionsSchema.init` line 222-255: creates `Constants.ADMIN_PERMISSIONS_CLIENT_ID` client, creates its `ResourceServer`, and creates all-clients resources for each resource type (line 247-252: `resourceServerRep.setResources(SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().keySet().stream().map(type -> { ResourceRepresentation resource = new ResourceRepresentation(type, ...); resource.setType(type); return resource; }).collect(Collectors.toList())))`). So the "Clients" all-clients resource exists by default in every V2 realm.
Step 4: V2 line 214: `resource = resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())` — looks up per-client resource on the realm server. If null (client never had V1-style `initialize()` called, or migration didn't create per-client resources), falls back to all-clients at line 217.
Step 5: V2 line 219: `if (authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()) { return false; }` — only denies if NO policies exist on the all-clients resource. If any policy exists (e.g. admin configured a permission via the admin console), evaluation proceeds.
findings.suggestion: Document the migration impact: under V2, clients with no per-client resource are **no longer deny-by-default** — they are governed by the all-clients "Clients" resource permission. Admins upgrading from V1 should be advised that (a) the all-clients resource is created automatically by `AdminPermissionsSchema.init`, (b) any permission configured on that resource applies to ALL clients, and (c) clients that were previously inaccessible (no per-client permissions enabled) may become accessible if an all-clients permission is configured. Consider adding a test that verifies the default state: a fresh V2 realm with no permissions configured on the all-clients resource denies `canManage`/`canView` for all clients (confirming the `policyStore.findByResource(...).isEmpty()` gate at line 219 works correctly).
findings.title: V2 hasPermission uses realm-level ResourceServer while V1 uses per-client ResourceServer — changes which ResourceServer scopes/policies are visible

findings.blocking_reason: Test code quality issue about cleanup specificity; does not break build, tests, or production behavior.
findings.body: The @AfterEach onAfter() method cleans ALL scope permissions via getScopePermissionsResource(client).findAll(null,null,null,-1,-1).forEach(...). This is over-broad because testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient creates USERS permissions (in addition to CLIENTS permissions), and the cleanup removes them all. While this doesn't cause test failures (since each test creates its own permissions), it masks potential cross-resource-type permission contamination: if a CLIENTS test inadvertently creates a USERS permission, the cleanup would remove it silently. The same pattern exists in UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest. A more targeted cleanup (filtering by resourceType) would be safer and more explicit.
findings.evidence: Line 40-50: `getScopePermissionsResource(client).findAll(null,null,null,-1,-1)` — null resourceType filter means ALL resource types. Compare with createUserPolicy in AbstractPermissionTest which uses targeted realm.cleanup().add() for each policy.
findings.suggestion: Filter the cleanup by resource type: `getScopePermissionsResource(client).findAll(null, null, clientsType, -1, -1).forEach(...)` for CLIENTS tests. Or use the realm.cleanup() mechanism (as createUserPolicy does) to register targeted cleanup for each permission created.
findings.title: @AfterEach cleans ALL scope permissions — over-broad cleanup may mask cross-test contamination

findings.blocking_reason: The finding itself acknowledges the missing guard is 'defensive rather than functional' and the cross-resource scope-bleeding path is only theoretical, with no concrete demonstration that the evaluation engine returns permissions for unrelated resources.
findings.dimension_name: V2 hasPermission fall-back grants where V1 denies
findings.evidence:
Step 1: `ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` line 226-231: iterates permissions with NO resourceId check — `for (Permission permission : permissions) { for (String s : permission.getScopes()) { if (expectedScopes.contains(s)) { return true; } } }`.
Step 2: `UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission(UserModel, EvaluationContext, String...)` line 134-141: iterates permissions WITH resourceId check — `for (Permission permission : permissions) { if (permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId())) { for (String scope : permission.getScopes()) { if (expectedScopes.contains(scope)) { return true; } } } }`.
Step 3: `AdminPermissionsSchema` lines 67-68: `USERS = new ResourceType(USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE, Set.of(MANAGE, VIEW, IMPERSONATE, MAP_ROLES, MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP))` and `CLIENTS = new ResourceType(CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, Set.of(CONFIGURE, MANAGE, MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, VIEW))` — both share `MANAGE`, `VIEW`, `MAP_ROLES` scope names.
Step 4: The same unguarded pattern repeats in `ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(String)` (line 251-256) and `hasGrantedPermission(Resource, String)` (line 277-283).
findings.suggestion: Add the `permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId())` guard to `ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` (and to `hasPermission(String)` at line 249-257 and `hasGrantedPermission(Resource, String)` at line 274-285) to match `UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission`. This is a defensive consistency fix that closes a theoretical cross-resource-type scope-bleeding path.
findings.title: hasPermission(ClientModel, String) lacks resourceId guard present in UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission

findings.blocking_reason: This is a missing test coverage suggestion for an edge case, not a demonstrated production defect or contract break.
findings.body: testViewAllClients tests VIEW at the all-clients level (createAllPermission), verifying that VIEW grants listing and protocol mapper access but denies creation. However, no test grants VIEW-only on a single client and then attempts MANAGE operations (update, removeDefaultClientScope, addDefaultClientScope). The per-client VIEW → MANAGE denial path is untested. If the V2 evaluator incorrectly allows MANAGE operations when only VIEW is granted on a specific client, no test would catch it. testManageOnlyOneClient tests MANAGE (which should imply VIEW), but the reverse (VIEW does not imply MANAGE) is not tested at the single-client level.
findings.evidence: testViewAllClients (line 240-270) uses createAllPermission for all-clients VIEW. testManageOnlyOneClient (line 120-190) grants MANAGE. No test grants single-client VIEW-only and attempts MANAGE operations.
findings.suggestion: Add a test method that: (1) Grants only VIEW on myclient (not MANAGE), (2) Verifies myadmin can toRepresentation() and findAll(), (3) Verifies myadmin CANNOT update the client, (4) Verifies myadmin CANNOT removeDefaultClientScope or addDefaultClientScope.
findings.title: No single-client VIEW-only test attempting MANAGE operations — VIEW boundary on per-client untested

findings.blocking_reason: Test quality issue about null body possibly not exercising intended authorization path; no production impact demonstrated.
findings.body: In testViewAllClients, line 320 calls clients().create(null) to verify that VIEW-only permission denies client creation. However, passing a null body may cause the server to reject the request at the deserialization/validation layer BEFORE reaching the authorization check. This means the test could pass (getting FORBIDDEN or even BAD_REQUEST) without actually exercising the V2 permission evaluator's handling of the create operation under VIEW-only permissions. The test should use a valid ClientRepresentation body to ensure the request reaches the authorization layer.
findings.evidence: Line 320: `assertThrows(ForbiddenException.class, () -> realmAdminClient.clients().create(null))` — null body. Compare with testManageAllClients line 220 which correctly uses a valid ClientRepresentation for creation.
findings.suggestion: Replace `clients().create(null)` with `clients().create(ClientBuilder.create().clientId("test-client").build())` (or equivalent valid representation) to ensure the request passes deserialization and reaches the authorization check. Then assert FORBIDDEN is returned.
findings.title: testViewAllClients uses clients().create(null) — null body may not exercise authorization path

findings.blocking_reason: This is a UI display quality issue (showing raw UUIDs instead of names) with no demonstrated impact on build, security, data integrity, or API contracts.
findings.body: not `CLIENTS`. Per-client Resources fall through to `getDisplayName()` which is null → admin UI shows raw UUIDs. All findings verified against direct code reads of `ClientPermissionsV2.java`, `ClientPermissions.java` (V1), `AdminPermissionsSchema.java`, `UserPermissionsV2.java`, and `AuthorizationProvider.java`.
findings.dimension_name: Resource name resolution consistency between schema and per-client lookup
findings.title: `AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName` only handles `USERS` type

findings.blocking_reason: Test-only code consistency suggestion with no demonstrated production impact.
findings.body: In UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest, the same user's ID is accessed via two different patterns within the same test class: (1) Line 86: userAlice.admin().toRepresentation().getId() — fetches a fresh UserRepresentation from the server and extracts the ID. (2) Line 107: userAlice.getId() — uses the ManagedUser's cached ID. While these should return the same value, the inconsistency is a code smell that could mask issues if the ManagedUser cache becomes stale or if the admin client's representation differs. The refactoring from createUserPermission(UserRepresentation, ...) to createPermission(client, String resourceId, ...) changed the call sites but left inconsistent ID access patterns.
findings.evidence: Line 86: createPermission(client, userAlice.admin().toRepresentation().getId(), usersType, Set.of(VIEW), policy). Line 107: createPermission(client, Logic.NEGATIVE, myadmin.getId(), usersType, Set.of(IMPERSONATE)). Two different patterns for the same conceptual operation.
findings.suggestion: Standardize on userAlice.getId() (the ManagedUser cached ID) throughout the test class, since ManagedUser guarantees the ID is stable. Remove unnecessary server round-trips via admin().toRepresentation().getId() unless the test specifically needs a fresh fetch.
findings.title: Inconsistent user ID access patterns — userAlice.admin().toRepresentation().getId() vs userAlice.getId()

findings.blocking_reason: The finding explicitly states this is not a correctness bug and only describes an unnecessary store query, which is a performance nitpick.
findings.body: At line 83, `resourceStore.findById(resourceServer, id)` attempts a lookup by resource primary key. For the CLIENTS resource type, `id` is a client storage id (or clientId), not a resource id. Since resources are created via `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, server.getClientId())` (line 104) with an auto-generated resource id, the client id will never match a resource primary key. This makes the findById call at line 83 a guaranteed no-op (returns null) for the CLIENTS path, before the code proceeds to resolveClient (line 91) and findByName (line 101). The findById fast-path appears designed for import scenarios where `id` IS a resource id (AuthorizationProvider.java line 304 and RepresentationToModel.java line 1423 pass representation ids), but for CLIENTS it is wasted I/O. Not a correctness bug — the code falls through correctly to findByName — but it adds an unnecessary store query per CLIENTS permission operation.
findings.evidence: AdminPermissionsSchema.java:83 — `resourceStore.findById(resourceServer, id)` where id is the raw input (client storage id for CLIENTS type). AdminPermissionsSchema.java:104 — `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, server.getClientId())` creates with auto-generated id, not the input id. Callers: AuthorizationProvider.java:304 and RepresentationToModel.java:1423 pass `id` from representation/policy objects (resource ids for import, client ids for CLIENTS).
findings.suggestion: Consider gating the findById fast-path (line 83) so it only executes when resourceType != CLIENTS (and != USERS, if the same pattern applies), or document that findById is intentional for import-id reuse and accepts the no-op cost for CLIENTS. Alternatively, verify whether any import path actually sets a resource's primary key to a client id — if not, the findById path could be removed for CLIENTS to avoid unnecessary store queries on hot permission-check paths.
findings.title: getOrCreateResource findById fast-path is a no-op for CLIENTS resource type

findings.blocking_reason: Code style and consistency issue with no production correctness, security, or API contract impact.
findings.body: After the refactoring, AbstractPermissionTest has a mixed static/instance pattern: createUserPolicy, createClientPolicy, createAllPermission, getPermissionsResource, getScopePermissionsResource, and createPermission(ManagedClient, ScopePermissionRepresentation) are static. However, createPermission(ManagedClient, resourceId, resourceType, scopes, policies...) and its Logic overload are instance methods (they use getPolicies() which is also instance). Additionally, getPolicies() remains an instance method while getPermissionsResource(client) is static. This inconsistency makes the API harder to reason about — callers must know which methods require an instance and which don't. The instance methods could be made static by passing the ManagedRealm as a parameter (similar to how createUserPolicy takes realm).
findings.evidence: Static: createUserPolicy(realm, client, name, userId), createClientPolicy(realm, client, name, clientId), createAllPermission(client, resourceType, policy, scopes). Instance: createPermission(client, resourceId, resourceType, scopes, policies...) — delegates to getPolicies() which is instance. Mixed pattern in same class.
findings.suggestion: Either make createPermission(client, resourceId, ...) and its Logic overload static by passing ManagedRealm as an additional parameter (matching createUserPolicy's pattern), or make all helpers instance methods. Choose one pattern and apply consistently.
findings.title: Mixed static/instance method pattern — createPermission is instance while createUserPolicy/createClientPolicy/createAllPermission are static
